newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. Africa's Pan Africanist Congress names leader.
newsitem.headline: S. Africa's Pan Africanist Congress names leader.

text.p: Bishop Stanley Mogoba, former head of the Methodist Church in South Africa, was on Monday elected president of the black-supremacist Pan Africanist Congress (PAC).
PAC officials said Mogoba was elected unopposed after veteran party leader Clarence Makwetu gave up his fight to retain the position in the early hours of Monday.
They said PAC delegates meeting in Tohoyandou, north of Johannesburg, also authorised a police probe of alleged mismanagement of party funds.

Makwetu, who helped to found the party in 1959 and was jailed with President Nelson Mandela on Robben Island for opposing white rule, refused to step down after the PAC's poor showing in the first all-race elections in April 1994.

The party was founded by African National Congress members dissatisfied with the high-profile role of whites in the movement and with the ANC's alliance with other groups, including the South African Communist Party.

The PAC, which campaigned mainly on a black supremacist platform and a demand for the return of land taken from blacks since the first white settlers arrived in 1652, secured only five of the 400 seats in parliament with 1.25 percent of the vote.

PAC officials said Makwetu fought to the end on Monday to prevent his ouster, challenging nomination procedures and threatening legal action against the party, but withdrew after midnight when it became clear he could not win.
Mogoba stepped down earlier this month as head of the Methodist church, which counts Mandela among its members, saying the party needed him.

Mogoba was among priests, including Anglican Archbishop Desmond Tutu, who used the relative immunity of their positions to voice opposition to apartheid when South Africa's white leaders used a state of emergency to silence most dissent.
